items.stem: What is the receiver and return value of the scope function apply?

options.text: Receiver is this; it returns the same object after running the block
options.rationale: apply runs the block with the object as this and returns that object, ideal for configuration.

options.text: Receiver is it; it returns the block's last expression

options.rationale: apply returns the receiver object, not Unit.
apply returns the object, so it chains naturally.

items.stem: Select TWO reasons to prefer a Sequence over a List for a long transformation pipeline in Kotlin.

options.text: Operations are evaluated lazily, element by element
options.rationale: Sequences avoid building an intermediate collection per step.

options.text: It avoids allocating an intermediate collection at each step
options.rationale: Lazy evaluation processes one element through the whole chain.
Sequences are not parallel by default.

options.text: It guarantees the result is sorted
options.rationale: Sequences do not sort unless you ask them to.

items.explanation: Sequences avoid building an intermediate collection per step.

items.stem: Why does an exhaustive when over a sealed class not need an else branch?

options.text: The compiler knows all subclasses, so covering each makes the when complete
options.rationale: Sealed hierarchies are closed, enabling exhaustiveness checking.

options.text: else is never allowed with sealed classes
options.rationale: else is allowed but unnecessary when all cases are covered.

options.text: Sealed classes can only have one subclass
options.rationale: They can have many, all known at compile time.
Exhaustive when expressions over sealed types do not require else.

items.explanation: Sealed hierarchies are closed, enabling exhaustiveness checking.
